question: When fats become institutions — laws, sacrifices, gymnasia — which fat belongs to which civilisation?
summary: This is the period in which the olive becomes Greek, ghee becomes Indian and the northern butter becomes a mark of barbarism. At Ekron in Philistia a purpose-built quarter of over a hundred presses shows industrial oil in the 600s BC ([[ec1]]); in Athens an estimated 200–330 kg of olive oil a year goes through a wealthy household for food, lamps and the body ([[ec2]], [[te2]], [[te3]]), the Panathenaic prizes carry the goddess's oil ([[b3]]) and Solon is said to have let Attica export only oil ([[o1]]). The sacred olives are protected by law and honoured in myth, and the prize oil alone runs to 1,113 amphorae ([[o2]], [[b4]], [[ec6]]). The beam press is the Greek machine ([[te1]]).

India offers the contrasting culture: the Vedic sacrifice makes ghee a ‘commodity of enormous prestige’ ([[b1]]), sesame is one of the nine sacred grains ([[b2]]), and mustard and safflower are named as oil sources ([[ec3]]). Sesame also moves west and north, to Babylon's only oil in Herodotus ([[th1]]), a workshop at Karmir Blur ([[ec4]]) and a Macedonian tavern ([[ec5]]).

Between these oil cultures lies a fat frontier. A Greek comic poet mocks the Thracians as ‘butter eaters’ ([[e1]]); the Zhou court cooks each meat in its own animal fat, since no oil was pressed in China before the Han ([[th2]]); and the origin of the olive in Italy and the west is still argued ([[x1]]).

The folio is wider than Athens and the Ganges. Egypt’s pharaoh plants olive groves to keep Ra’s lamps burning and Judah sends Tekoa’s oil to the Temple ([[b6]], [[b5]]); in India the Buddha lets a sick monk eat animal fats, texts fry in ghee and the ghani may be as old as the 700s BC ([[b7]], [[ec10]], [[te5]]); and in Africa a Niger Delta core shows oil-palm pollen surging about 850 BC, which its author reads as forest clearance ([[ec11]]). The Athenian figures also come with a warning from Foxhall: oil yields swing from year to year, so Attica did not specialise ([[ec8]], [[ec9]]).

themes.title: The Greek olive: an economy and a body
text: Presses, consumption figures, lamps and the gymnasium show oil as food, light and cleanser at once, and Athena's trees make it sacred. Solon's export law is the earliest state measure on oil, but its authenticity is disputed.

themes.title: The sacred oil, from Athena to Ra
text: Athens, Judah and Egypt each build a religious claim on lamp and temple oil, while the Athenian state legislates for its sacred trees and awards oil as prizes.

themes.title: Industrial oil in the Near East
text: Ekron's hundred presses and Karmir Blur's sesame workshop are the largest known oil works of the Iron Age; Herodotus's Babylon uses sesame, not olive oil.

themes.title: India: ghee, sesame and the sacred
text: Ghee fries food and feeds the sacred fire; sesame is a sacred grain; oil is a growing alternative by the Sutra period.

themes.title: Where the frontier runs
text: Butter against oil in Greek comedy; animal fat against pressed oil in China; the olive's western spread.

themes.title: Africa’s oil palm
text: A single pollen core: the only African evidence of this period in the folio, and an interpretation (clearance by farmers, not climate) that other palynologists question.

turning_points.text: Oil-palm pollen surges in the Niger Delta.
A sesame-oil workshop is built at Karmir Blur.
Solon allows only olive oil to be exported from Attica.
Athens awards 1,113 amphorae of prize oil.
The beam press is the Greek machine for oil and wine.
Herodotus: the Babylonians use only sesame oil.
A Greek comedy calls the Thracians ‘butter eaters’.

how_to_read: Start with the Greek entries in *Economy* and *Technology*, which are the best-quantified in the folio, then *Belief* for the Indian ghee and sesame. The Nexus links the household oil figures to lamps, the gymnasium and the sacred.
China is the contrast: look at *Thought* for the Zhou fats before the next folio's first pressing of seeds.

The *picture by region* shows how Greek the folio is: sixteen entries are Greek or western, seven Indian, five Near Eastern, one African. That is the shape of the library, not of the ancient world; the gaps paragraph says what is missing.

sources.intro: The Greek half rests on one excellent book; the Indian and Chinese halves on a translated reference work each; the Near Eastern industrial sites on a journalist's summary and an atlas folio.
main: Foxhall, *Olive Cultivation in Ancient Greece*, for Athens, the press and the lamp ([[ec2]], [[te1]], [[te2]], [[te3]], [[b3]], [[o1]], [[x1]]).
Achaya, *Indian Food Tradition*, for ghee, sesame and mustard oil ([[b1]], [[b2]], [[ec3]]).
Needham, SCC 6.5, for the Zhou fats ([[th2]]); Bedigian for sesame in Babylon and Urartu ([[th1]], [[ec4]], [[ec5]]).
Mueller and the atlas folio on Philistia for Ekron ([[ec1]]); Khosrova for the butter eaters ([[e1]]).

Foxhall again for the sacred olives, prize oil and the crusher ([[o2]], [[b4]], [[ec6]], [[ec8]], [[ec9]], [[te4]]); Mueller for Tekoa, Ra’s groves and the burned olive ([[b5]], [[b6]], [[b4]]); Achaya and Needham for the ghani and ghee frying ([[ec10]], [[te5]], [[b7]]); Kiple, after Sowunmi, for the Niger Delta ([[ec11]]).
contested: Solon's law ([[o1]]) and the question of who brought the olive west ([[x1]]).
The Athenian household figures are an estimate, not a record ([[ec2]]).
The Zhou li passage was compiled later than the period it describes ([[th2]]).

The date of the Lysias speech is conventional ([[o2]]); the Ra papyrus is dated to Ramses II about 1000 BC by Mueller and usually to Ramses III about 1150 BC ([[b6]]); the Niger Delta pollen is read as clearance, not climate, by one author ([[ec11]]).
gaps: Phoenician and Carthaginian roles in spreading the olive are only touched ([[x1]]); Egypt under the Ptolemies is in the next folio.
Africa has one entry: nothing here on Nubia, Meroe, Carthage’s own oil or the Sahara, and the library holds little on sub-Saharan Africa before 1500.
Chinese oils are covered only through Needham, India only through Achaya; Central Asia, Southeast Asia, the Americas and Oceania have no entry.

text: Sixteen entries, almost all Greek: Athens’s laws, myths and prizes for the sacred olive, a wealthy household’s oil, the beam press and the rotary crusher, the strigil, a Macedonian tavern’s sesame, and the unsettled question of who brought the olive west ([[o1]], [[o2]], [[b3]], [[b4]], [[ec6]], [[ec2]], [[te1]], [[te4]], [[te3]], [[ec5]], [[x1]]). Foxhall warns that Attica did not specialise in oil ([[ec8]]).
Industrial oil at Ekron and sesame at Karmir Blur, Herodotus’s Babylon, and the sacred oil of Judah and Egypt ([[ec1]], [[ec4]], [[th1]], [[b5]], [[b6]]). Egypt is filed here by the atlas taxonomy.

India: ghee in the Vedic sacrifice, sesame as a sacred grain, mustard and safflower, the Buddha’s fats for the sick, frying in ghee and the ghani ([[b1]], [[b2]], [[ec3]], [[b7]], [[ec10]], [[te5]]); China appears only as the Zhou court cooking each meat in its own fat ([[th2]]).

One entry: the Niger Delta pollen core, read as oil-palm farming about 850 BC ([[ec11]]). Egypt’s lamp groves and the Nile sit under the Near East. The library has little on sub-Saharan Africa before 1500.
No entry. Nothing in the library bears on American fats in 1200–300 BC beyond the folio before this one (peanut, sunflower).
No entry. The Pacific coconut is first placed in the folio that follows.
